newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh -- from model soldier to convicted bomber.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh -- from model soldier to convicted bomber.

text.p: Thin, tall and clean-cut, he looks like an all-American boy and he grew up playing Little League baseball and joining the Army, just like millions of others.

But a jury found on Monday that Timothy McVeigh was what one biographer termed the "All-American Monster" -- the man who planned and carried out the bombing of the Oklahoma City federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
Jurors found, agreeing with prosecutors, that McVeigh's American dream was a nightmare -- to blow up a building full of government workers to foment a second American Revolution.

One prosecution witness, a former McVeigh friend, testified that he considered the people inside the Alfred P. Murrah federal building "individually innocent but collectively part of the evil empire."

After promising in pre-trial interviews that he would testify, McVeigh remained silent in his defence with his thoughts and actions described by reluctant witnesses for the prosecution -- his sister, an ex-roommate, his former best friend and the friend's wife.

Even they had nice things to say about him. "If you don't consider what happened in Oklahoma, Tim was a good person," said star prosecution witness Michael Fortier, who testified against McVeigh in hopes of avoiding a lengthy jail term for himself and any jail time for his wife Lori.

Lori Fortier said McVeigh showed her one day how he would make the bomb that destroyed the Murrah building. Using soup cans, he told her to pretend they were barrels of explosives, but she said she did not believe he would or could do it.
But she also said she helped make a false drivers license for him under the name of Robert Kling that he used to rent the truck used in the bombing.

Before court sessions started, McVeigh would flash boyish grins at his lawyers and sometimes he would laugh at the jokes made by prosecution lawyers who goal was to convince a jury he should be executed.

His sister Jennifer told the court of his obsession with "The Turner Diaries," a racist, anti-Semitic novel in which extremists blow up FBI headquarters to start a second American Revolution. He sent her sections of the book and in a letter to her he declared he had moved from "the propaganda stage to the action stage."

McVeigh was once a promising young soldier who won a Bronze Star in the Gulf War. He had an ordinary childhood, growing up in Pendleton, a small town in western New York state. He excelled in the Army, where his obsession with neatness and fitness impressed commanders.

But his life seemed to fall apart when he left the Army soon after he failed to get into the elite Special Forces. He drifted around the country, becoming increasingly drawn to far right politics, finding inspiration in "The Turner Diaries" and films like "Star Wars."

He also grew increasingly obsessed with the government showdown with the Branch Davidian sect in Waco, Texas, in which some 80 people died. McVeigh blamed the government and during his trial Fortier testified that McVeigh thought the showdown at Waco was planned in the Murrah building.
It was bombed two years to the day after Waco.
Born on April 23, 1968, McVeigh was the son of William McVeigh, an autoworker. His parents divorced when he was 10 years old and his mother moved to Florida without him.

McVeigh developed an early passion for guns, shooting in woods near his home. At 14 he told friends he was a survivalist, stockpiling food and weapons "in case of a nuclear attack or the communists took over the country," according to The Washington Post.

After graduating from high school, he did several jobs, including working as a security guard for an armoured truck company, before joining the Army in 1988. During basic training he became close friends with Terry Nichols, who was also charged with the bombing. Nichols will be tried later.

McVeigh scored high on tests, kept his uniform neatly pressed and volunteered for extra duties, winning rapid promotion to sergeant. Some colleagues thought he was destined for a brilliant military career. But fellow soldiers told The New York Times McVeigh assigned "dirty work" around barracks to black soldiers.

After leaving the army, he found work as a security guard in Buffalo. He showed his frustration with the government in a 1992 letter to a local newspaper that said: "Do we have to shed blood to reform the current system? I hope it doesn't come to that! But it might."
A reporter for that paper, Brandon Stickney, wrote a biography of McVeigh, calling it, "All American Monster." The jury in Denver on Monday found him guilty on all counts.
